# Frustration-Induced One-Dimensionalization as a Mechanism for Gapless Spin Liquid Behavior

## Motivation

This study is motivated by the experimental observation of a gapless spin liquid state in the organic material κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃. This compound has attracted considerable attention because it fails to develop long-range magnetic order down to very low temperatures, instead exhibiting the hallmarks of a spin liquid ground state characterized by gapless magnetic excitations. Understanding the microscopic origin of this behavior poses a significant theoretical challenge and provides the primary impetus for the present work.

## Model and Theoretical Approach

To investigate this phenomenon, the researchers analyze the anisotropic triangular lattice S = 1/2 Heisenberg model, which serves as an appropriate minimal description of the magnetic degrees of freedom in this material. Their analysis employs the resonating valence bond (RVB) mean-field approximation, a framework well suited to capturing the physics of spin liquid states in frustrated quantum magnets.

A key feature of their approach is the treatment of the system as an array of one-dimensional chains that are coupled together by frustrating zig-zag bonds. This decomposition reflects the intrinsic quasi-one-dimensional anisotropy present in the real material, where the magnetic exchange interactions are stronger along certain directions than others.

## Results

By systematically varying the anisotropy parameter J′/J, the researchers interpolate between two limiting cases: the regime of decoupled one-dimensional chains and the fully isotropic triangular lattice. Across this entire range, they find that the excitations remain almost gapless, extending over a wide parameter window that begins at the one-dimensional limit. This robustness of gapless excitations is a central result of their analysis.

## Conclusion

Based on these findings, the authors propose a mechanism they term "one-dimensionalization by frustration." In this picture, the frustrating interchain interactions effectively reinforce the one-dimensional character of the system rather than driving it toward conventional ordered states, thereby stabilizing gapless excitations over a broad range of anisotropies. This mechanism is put forward as a compelling candidate for explaining the gapless spin liquid state observed in κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃.

# Gapless Spin Liquid in the Anisotropic Triangular Lattice: A Resonating Valence Bond Analysis

## Introduction and Motivation

The discovery of a gapless spin liquid state in the organic Mott insulator κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃ has generated considerable interest in understanding the microscopic mechanisms that can stabilize such exotic quantum states. In this material, the absence of magnetic ordering down to temperatures far below the exchange coupling energy scale, combined with thermodynamic signatures indicative of low-energy excitations, points to a spin liquid ground state lacking a spin gap. This behavior stands in contrast to conventional expectations for two-dimensional magnets and demands a theoretical framework capable of explaining how gapless excitations can persist across the relevant parameter regime.

The essential physics of κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃ is well captured by the S=1/2 Heisenberg model on an anisotropic triangular lattice. This lattice geometry naturally interpolates between two important limiting cases: the isotropic triangular lattice, characterized by strong geometric frustration, and the decoupled one-dimensional chain system. The interplay between reduced dimensionality and frustration in this model provides fertile ground for the emergence of unconventional ground states.

## Theoretical Approach

In this work, we analyze the anisotropic triangular lattice Heisenberg model using a resonating valence bond (RVB) mean-field approximation. Rather than approaching the problem from the two-dimensional square-lattice or isotropic-triangular limit, we adopt a perspective that begins from the one-dimensional chains. In this picture, the well-understood physics of decoupled spin chains serves as the starting point, and the chains are then coupled together through frustrating zig-zag bonds that connect neighboring chains in a staggered fashion.

This choice of reference point is physically motivated: one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg chains are known to host gapless spinon excitations, described by a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid with a characteristic linear excitation spectrum. By treating the interchain coupling as a frustrating perturbation within the RVB framework, we can systematically track how the gapless character of the one-dimensional system evolves as the anisotropy parameter is varied toward the more two-dimensional regime.

## Results

We compute the one-particle excitation spectra within the RVB mean-field decoupling. Our central finding is that the excitations remain almost gapless across a wide range of the anisotropy parameter, extending well beyond the strict one-dimensional limit. In other words, the frustrating zig-zag couplings do not immediately open a substantial spin gap; instead, the system retains the essentially gapless character inherited from its one-dimensional constituents over an extended region of parameter space.

This robustness of the gapless spectrum can be understood as a consequence of the frustration itself. The zig-zag geometry of the interchain bonds suppresses the tendency toward magnetic ordering and confinement that would otherwise accompany interchain coupling. As a result, the frustration effectively preserves the one-dimensional-like behavior of the excitations, a phenomenon we describe as "one-dimensionalization by frustration."

## Discussion and Conclusion

Our results suggest that this frustration-induced one-dimensionalization is a viable candidate mechanism for the gapless spin liquid state observed in κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃. By retaining the gapless spinon excitations characteristic of one-dimensional chains over a broad range of two-dimensional anisotropy, the model naturally accounts for the absence of a spin gap in the experimental system.

This scenario offers an appealing alternative to purely two-dimensional descriptions of the spin liquid state, emphasizing the crucial role played by the combination of low dimensionality and geometric frustration. Further theoretical and experimental investigation of the excitation spectra and their anisotropy dependence would help to establish whether this mechanism fully describes the low-energy physics of κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃ and related frustrated organic materials.

# BEDT-TTF: A Molecule That Continues to Motivate Researchers

Few organic molecules have captured the sustained attention of chemists and physicists quite like **BEDT-TTF**, formally known as bis(ethylenedithio)tetrathiafulvalene. Often abbreviated simply as ET, this sulfur-rich organic compound has become a cornerstone in the study of molecular conductors and superconductors, and researchers remain highly **motivated** to explore its remarkable properties.

## From TTF to BEDT-TTF

The story begins with **TTF** (tetrathiafulvalene), a small planar molecule that proved to be an excellent electron donor. When TTF combines with strong electron acceptors, it can form charge-transfer salts that conduct electricity—a surprising quality for organic materials, which are typically insulators. This discovery opened an entirely new field of research.

BEDT-TTF represents an evolution of the original TTF framework. By adding two ethylenedithio groups to the TTF core, chemists created a molecule with enhanced sulfur–sulfur interactions. These interactions allow the molecules to pack closely together in the solid state, forming extended networks through which electrons can travel more freely.

## Why Researchers Stay Motivated

Several factors explain the enduring scientific interest in BEDT-TTF:

- **Superconductivity:** Certain BEDT-TTF salts become superconductors at low temperatures, making them valuable models for understanding how superconductivity arises in low-dimensional systems.
- **Structural diversity:** BEDT-TTF forms numerous crystalline phases (labeled α, β, κ, θ, and others), each with distinct electronic behavior. This variety provides a rich playground for studying structure–property relationships.
- **Tunable properties:** By changing the counter-anions or applying pressure, scientists can shift these materials between insulating, metallic, and superconducting states.

## A Lasting Legacy

The continued exploration of BEDT-TTF reflects the broader appeal of organic electronics. As researchers pursue lighter, more flexible, and chemically adjustable materials, molecules like BEDT-TTF serve as both practical building blocks and fundamental research tools. Motivated by the promise of new discoveries, the scientific community continues to build upon the foundational chemistry of TTF and its celebrated derivative, ensuring that BEDT-TTF remains a subject of active and inspiring investigation.

## Abstract

We present a comprehensive analysis of the one-particle excitation spectra of the spin-1/2 anisotropic triangular Heisenberg antiferromagnet as a function of the interchain-to-intrachain coupling ratio J'/J, interpolating between the limit of decoupled one-dimensional chains (J'/J = 0) and the fully frustrated isotropic triangular lattice (J'/J = 1). Employing a combination of complementary techniques—including series expansion methods, spin-wave theory with 1/S corrections, and numerical approaches—we track the evolution of the dynamical structure factor and the character of the elementary excitations across this crossover.

In the decoupled-chain limit, the spectrum is dominated by the well-known two-spinon continuum characteristic of the one-dimensional Heisenberg model, with deconfined fractional excitations and vanishing single-magnon spectral weight. As J'/J increases, weak interchain coupling induces a gradual confinement of spinons: spectral weight redistributes from the incoherent continuum toward a coherent, sharply dispersing single-magnon branch, signaling the onset of long-range spiral magnetic order. We characterize the momentum-dependent transfer of spectral weight and the emergence of well-defined quasiparticle poles, identifying the energy scales at which coherent magnon excitations stabilize.

Approaching the isotropic limit, frustration strongly renormalizes the magnon dispersion, producing pronounced roton-like minima and substantial downward shifts relative to linear spin-wave predictions. We find persistent broad continua and anomalous spectral features at high energies, indicative of significant magnon decay and residual fractionalization, suggesting proximity to a quantum-disordered or spin-liquid regime. These signatures reflect the strong quantum fluctuations enhanced by the geometric frustration of the triangular geometry.

Our results establish a unified picture of the spinon-to-magnon crossover in quasi-one-dimensional frustrated magnets and provide quantitative benchmarks for interpreting inelastic neutron scattering experiments on materials such as Cs₂CuCl₄ and related organic triangular-lattice compounds.

In this scenario, geometric frustration dynamically decouples an intrinsically two-dimensional lattice into a system of weakly coupled one-dimensional chains, whose low-energy physics is governed by the well-understood Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid. We further discuss how quantum fluctuations and residual interchain frustration may either stabilize this one-dimensionalized state or drive instabilities toward incommensurate order, and we identify concrete predictions—such as characteristic scaling exponents and the momentum dependence of spinon continua—that distinguish this mechanism from competing scenarios based on resonating valence bond states or spinon Fermi surfaces. Our proposal offers a unifying, analytically tractable perspective on how dimensional reduction driven purely by frustration can serve as a route to gapless spin liquid physics in two-dimensional quantum magnets.
